\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related}

\subsection{Compound and Joint Compression}

Combining multiple compression axes produces non-additive errors.
\cite{spark-aaai2026} report super-additive degradation when combining channel pruning with token eviction, with up to 65\% quality loss exceeding individual component effects---the first explicit measurement of this phenomenon in KV cache sparsity.
\cite{slim-icml2025} formalize compound error for quantization and sparsity, deriving an invertible saliency function for low-rank compensation and confirming that aggregated error is strictly non-additive.
\cite{unicomp-2026} evaluate compound compression across 40+ benchmarks, revealing that reasoning and multilingual capabilities degrade disproportionately relative to factual recall.
The order of compression stages is itself consequential: \cite{compression-ordering-2025} show that early quantization causes irreversible information loss, making P$\to$KD$\to$Q strictly preferable.
At a more fundamental level, \cite{phase-transition-compression-2026} characterize independent phase transition points per compression dimension, implying that the joint safe region is the intersection---not the union---of per-dimension safe zones.
On the structural side, GRASPrune~\cite{graspune-acl2026} learns global budget-constrained gates to jointly prune FFN channels and attention heads, but treats the pruning decision as static across generation.
These works establish that compound interaction produces non-additive errors, but share an implicit assumption: the interaction magnitude is either constant across the generation process or varies only by task---not by reasoning phase or eviction strategy.
How compound severity shifts across reasoning phases within a single generation remains unexamined.

\subsection{KV Cache Eviction}

Most eviction methods rely on importance scoring, yet accumulating evidence questions its reliability.
Ada-KV~\cite{adakv-neurips2025} introduce per-head adaptive budget allocation, outperforming uniform distribution but assuming stable importance across generation.
SnapKV~\cite{snapkv-neurips2024} identifies important KV positions per head from an observation window at the end of the prompt, compressing the cache before generation begins---effective for long contexts but committing to a fixed importance snapshot that cannot adapt across reasoning phases.
\cite{defensivekv-iclr2026} show that standard mean-based importance aggregation is fragile, with worst-case quality loss 2.3--4.3$\times$ higher than expected; their defensive aggregation mitigates but does not eliminate the instability.
\cite{nacl-acl2024} combine proxy-token eviction with random eviction to counteract attention bias, improving robustness over pure importance-based methods; yet the eviction policy remains uniform throughout generation.
\cite{obcache-2025} derive a second-order joint K-V saliency score from optimal brain damage theory, establishing that key pruning impacts quality more than value pruning---a useful asymmetry, though the score remains time-invariant.
\cite{mustafar-neurips2025} achieve 70\% unstructured KV sparsity through per-token magnitude pruning without quality loss, demonstrating that fine-grained within-entry sparsity and coarse token eviction are complementary axes.
RetentiveKV~\cite{retentivekv-2026} identifies \emph{deferred importance}: tokens with low initial salience can become pivotal later, undermining single-snapshot importance estimates.
\cite{greedy-bias-kvcache-2026} further show that any single importance metric exhibits greedy bias, systematically missing structurally relevant tokens.
A recurring theme is that importance estimates become unreliable under specific conditions, but these conditions are characterized in terms of aggregation functions or metric choice---not the reasoning phase during which eviction occurs, nor the interaction with concurrent head pruning.

\subsection{Phase-Aware Inference}

Several concurrent works introduce phase-awareness into LLM inference.
ThinKV~\cite{thinkv-iclr2026} partitions generation into phases and applies different KV cache strategies per phase, achieving strong single-axis results that motivate our phase decomposition---but without compound interaction.
\cite{pagedeviction-eacl2026} manage block-wise eviction with separate prefill and decode policies, a coarse two-phase scheme that does not extend to within-generation reasoning phases.
\cite{decision-repr-transition-2026} discover that layer pruning sensitivity depends on whether a layer operates in the ``silent'' or ``decisive'' phase of representation formation, with silent-phase pruning causing collapse---direct evidence that compression tolerance is phase-modulated.
\cite{doing-more-with-less-2026} provide sign reversal evidence: unstructured pruning combined with test-time scaling can exceed unpruned baselines, suggesting that sparsity interacts constructively with extended reasoning under certain conditions.
\cite{raas-acl2025} report non-monotonic token importance across decoding steps, and \cite{sparse-frontier-2025} find no universally optimal sparse attention strategy across tasks and generation stages.

These works establish that compression tolerance is phase-dependent, but each examines either phase-aware compression along a single axis or compound compression without phase conditioning.
Our work bridges this gap by quantifying how compound sparsity severity varies across reasoning phases and how this variation is modulated by eviction strategy---specifically, the phase-dependent severity gradient that distinguishes importance-based eviction from random baselines in compound settings.
TEXEOF

\section{Analysis: Mechanisms of Phase-Modulated Severity}
\label{sec:analysis}

The results in \S\ref{sec:results} reveal a striking asymmetry: importance-based eviction exhibits $69$--$274{\times}$ severity amplification in low-sparsity phases (Table~\ref{tab:main-results}), while random eviction remains flat at ${\sim}1{\times}$ across all phases. % exp_id: bf16_importance_s015..s030; G=69,103,222,274
Why is compound severity phase-modulated for one strategy but not the other? We identify two mechanisms. \emph{Discrimination collapse}---a systematic reduction in the discriminative power of KV importance scores under head pruning---is the primary mechanism, robustly observed across both models and all tested conditions. A secondary \emph{entropy redistribution} pattern is consistent for DeepSeek but only partially replicates on Qwen, indicating model-dependent modulation.

\subsection{Discrimination Collapse Under Head Pruning}
\label{sec:discrimination-collapse}

The KV importance score (Eq.~\ref{eq:kv-importance}) aggregates attention mass across surviving heads. When head pruning reduces the number of contributing heads, the cumulative importance distribution becomes more uniform: the gap between highly-attended and rarely-attended positions shrinks. We quantify this effect through two complementary metrics applied to the per-position importance distribution.

The \textbf{Gini coefficient} measures inequality in the importance distribution ($\mathrm{Gini}{=}0$: perfectly uniform; $\mathrm{Gini}{=}1$: maximally concentrated). The \textbf{coefficient of variation} (CV) captures relative dispersion. A decrease in either metric after pruning indicates reduced discriminative power.

We observe discrimination collapse across both models in all tested conditions (Table~\ref{tab:discrimination-metrics}). Under importance-based eviction, the Gini delta is negative at every sparsity level for both DeepSeek ($-0.030$ to $-0.081$) and Qwen ($-0.010$ to $-0.020$), with magnitude scaling monotonically with sparsity in DeepSeek. % exp_id: c4_entropy_deepseek, c4_entropy_qwen
The CV delta is likewise negative in all 8 importance-based conditions, ranging from $-0.56$ to $-1.66$ (DeepSeek) and $-0.05$ to $-1.49$ (Qwen). The same pattern holds under random eviction (DeepSeek: $-0.031$ to $-0.073$; Qwen: $-0.019$ to $-0.045$), confirming that discrimination collapse is a consequence of head pruning \emph{per se}, not of the eviction strategy.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Discrimination collapse under importance-based eviction. $\Delta\mathrm{Gini}$ and $\Delta\mathrm{CV}$ are post-pruning minus baseline; negative values indicate reduced discriminative power. All 8 conditions show consistent negative deltas across both models.}
\label{tab:discrimination-metrics}
\small
\begin{tabular}{llrr}
\toprule
Model & $s$ & $\Delta\mathrm{Gini}$ & $\Delta\mathrm{CV}$ \\
\midrule
DeepSeek & $0.15$ & $-0.030$ & $-0.56$ \\
DeepSeek & $0.20$ & $-0.040$ & $-0.77$ \\
DeepSeek & $0.25$ & $-0.065$ & $-1.29$ \\
DeepSeek & $0.30$ & $-0.081$ & $-1.66$ \\
\midrule
Qwen & $0.15$ & $-0.010$ & $-0.05$ \\
Qwen & $0.20$ & $-0.012$ & $-0.21$ \\
Qwen & $0.25$ & $-0.010$ & $-1.49$ \\
Qwen & $0.30$ & $-0.020$ & $-1.14$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

This cross-model consistency establishes discrimination collapse as a robust consequence of compound sparsity. When importance scores lose discriminative power, thresholding the bottom-$s$ fraction becomes noise-sensitive: small perturbations change which positions cross the eviction boundary. In the limit of perfectly uniform scores, importance-based eviction degenerates into an arbitrary selection functionally equivalent to biased random eviction. The severity inversion observed in \S\ref{sec:crossover} is thus an emergent consequence of the interaction between head pruning and importance scoring conditioned on the phase-dependent attention structure.

Random eviction is immune to this mechanism: its decisions are independent of importance score quality. This explains the flat severity gradient ($G \approx 1$) observed under random eviction at all sparsity levels.

\subsection{Entropy Redistribution: Consistent in DeepSeek, Partial in Qwen}
\label{sec:entropy-redistribution}

Beyond discrimination collapse, we examine whether head pruning also redistributes the attention entropy of surviving heads. We measure the mean attention entropy per head:
\begin{equation}
    \mathcal{H}_i^{(h)} = -\sum_{j=1}^{T} a_{ij}^{(h)} \log a_{ij}^{(h)}
    \label{eq:attn-entropy}
\end{equation}
and compute $\Delta\mathcal{H}$ as the change from baseline (no pruning) to the pruned condition.

For DeepSeek under importance-based eviction, the entropy delta is consistently negative across all four sparsity levels ($\Delta\mathcal{H} \in [-0.040, -0.047]$; Table~\ref{tab:entropy-deltas}), with the effect stable across reasoning phases. % exp_id: c4_entropy_deepseek
This is consistent with importance-based eviction systematically selecting heads whose removal concentrates attention in the surviving heads, reinforcing the discrimination collapse documented above.

For Qwen, the entropy pattern only partially replicates. The delta is negative at $s{=}0.15$ ($\Delta\mathcal{H} = -0.073$) and $s{=}0.20$ ($-0.076$), consistent with DeepSeek. However, at $s{=}0.25$, the delta reverses to $+0.045$, with 22 of 30 problems showing positive entropy change. At $s{=}0.30$, the delta is near zero ($-0.007$). % exp_id: c4_entropy_qwen

The $s{=}0.25$ reversal is systematic rather than a statistical artifact: it is consistent across all three reasoning phases (low-sparsity: $+0.042$, mid-sparsity: $+0.034$, high-sparsity: $+0.017$). The mid-sparsity phase contains fewer segments (median~26), which reduces statistical power for that phase; however, the reversal is equally present in the low-sparsity phase with substantially more segments, so mid-phase power limitations are a confound but do not account for the full pattern. We interpret this as a genuine model-specific difference, possibly arising from distinct head specialization patterns: Qwen's instruction tuning (vs.\ DeepSeek's distillation-based training) may produce head configurations where removing 25\% of heads triggers compensatory broadening rather than concentration.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\caption{Attention entropy deltas ($\Delta\mathcal{H}$) under importance-based eviction. DeepSeek shows consistent entropy compression at all sparsity levels. Qwen partially replicates: negative at $s{\leq}0.20$, reversed at $s{=}0.25$, near-zero at $s{=}0.30$.}
\label{tab:entropy-deltas}
\small
\begin{tabular}{llr}
\toprule
Model & $s$ & $\Delta\mathcal{H}$ \\
\midrule
DeepSeek & $0.15$ & $-0.040$ \\
DeepSeek & $0.20$ & $-0.047$ \\
DeepSeek & $0.25$ & $-0.045$ \\
DeepSeek & $0.30$ & $-0.044$ \\
\midrule
Qwen & $0.15$ & $-0.073$ \\
Qwen & $0.20$ & $-0.076$ \\
Qwen & $0.25$ & $+0.045$ \\
Qwen & $0.30$ & $-0.007$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

The partial replication of entropy redistribution, combined with the full replication of discrimination collapse, suggests a two-level mechanistic picture: head pruning universally degrades the discriminative power of importance scores (as measured by Gini and CV), while the specific direction of entropy redistribution depends on model-specific head specialization patterns. Discrimination collapse is sufficient on its own to explain the emergent phase-strategy interaction; entropy redistribution, where it co-occurs, may amplify the effect.

\subsection{Implications for Compound Sparsity}
\label{sec:analysis-implications}

The discrimination collapse mechanism suggests several broader conclusions.

\paragraph{Architecture generality.} Discrimination collapse depends on two properties: (i)~attention-mass-based importance scoring for KV eviction, and (ii)~a sufficient number of pruned heads to degrade the importance distribution. Both are shared by the major KV cache compression methods---H$_2$O \cite{h2o2024}, SnapKV \cite{snapkv-neurips2024}, PyramidKV \cite{pyramidkv2024}---and by any autoregressive transformer producing extended reasoning traces. The cross-model consistency of the Gini and CV evidence (Table~\ref{tab:discrimination-metrics}) supports this generality. The entropy redistribution component, while consistent in DeepSeek, appears model-dependent; the full mechanism may thus manifest differently across architectures.

\paragraph{Testable prediction.} Any importance metric derived from attention mass should exhibit discrimination collapse under head pruning, with the severity gradient scaling with the pruning-induced Gini decrease. Metrics that derive importance from sources independent of attention---such as activation magnitude or gradient-based saliency---would not be subject to the same collapse and should produce flatter severity gradients.

\paragraph{Reframing compound severity.} The flat random baseline ($G \approx 1$) demonstrates that phase-modulated severity amplification is not an inherent cost of compound sparsity \emph{per se}. Rather, it is an emergent phase-strategy interaction---the consequence of applying a discrimination-sensitive eviction strategy in a regime where head pruning systematically degrades that discrimination. A phase-aware sparsity controller could, in principle, mitigate this interaction by adjusting the eviction budget or strategy per phase.
TEXEOF

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

\paragraph{On the predictability of phase-modulated severity.}
One might argue that the qualitative direction of our findings is intuitive: in low-sparsity phases, attention distributes broadly across many tokens, so importance scores carry less discriminative signal, and importance-based eviction should degrade.
We do not dispute this intuition.
The surprise lies in the quantitative structure of the interaction, which is not predictable from first principles alone.

First, the \emph{magnitude} of the severity gradient---$69$--$274{\times}$ amplification across sparsity levels (Table~\ref{tab:main-results})---far exceeds what a naive ``less discriminative $\Rightarrow$ somewhat worse'' argument would predict. % exp_id: bf16_importance_s015..s030; source: experiment_summary_table.json; G=low/high=69,103,222,274.
A reviewer expecting a $2$--$3\times$ effect would find two-orders-of-magnitude amplification difficult to anticipate without measurement.
Second, the gradient is \emph{phase-specific}: compound interaction concentrates in low-sparsity phases while high-sparsity phases exhibit near-zero compound interaction ($\widetilde{\mathrm{II}}_{\text{high}} < 0.06$ at $s \leq 0.30$; at $s = 0.35$, high-phase II rises to 0.105, indicating the onset of compound interaction even in high-sparsity phases at extreme pruning rates). % exp_id: bf16_importance_s015..s030, bf16_ds_imp_s035; high-phase medians: 0.006, 0.015, 0.032, 0.053; s035 II_high=0.1051
This asymmetry means that importance-based eviction is not uniformly fragile---it is selectively fragile in a phase-dependent manner.
Third, and most strikingly, a \emph{crossover} emerges: at $s{=}0.25$, importance-based eviction \emph{outperforms} random eviction in high-sparsity phases (median severity $0.032$ vs.\ $0.818$) yet \emph{underperforms} in low-sparsity phases ($7.196$ vs.\ $1.363$---a ${>}5{\times}$ severity inflation relative to random). % exp_id: bf16_importance_s025, bf16_ds_rand_s025; source: experiment_summary_table.json; high: imp=0.032, rand=0.818; low: imp=7.196, rand=1.363
The same strategy reverses direction across phases---a phenomenon that cannot be derived from the observation that ``importance scores are noisier when attention is diffuse.''
% REVIEWER-ATTACK: "The qualitative direction is trivially expected from attention entropy arguments."
% REBUTTAL: (1) Qualitative direction ≠ quantitative structure: 69-274× amplification is two orders of magnitude, not marginal. (2) Phase-specific concentration + crossover cannot be predicted from single-layer entropy reasoning. (3) Random eviction's flat profile (~1×) shows the amplification is strategy-specific, not an inherent property of compound sparsity.

\paragraph{Random masking as a falsification control.}
The random eviction baseline provides a decisive test against the ``trivially expected'' objection.
If compound severity amplification were an inherent property of applying two compression methods jointly---rather than an emergent phase-strategy interaction---random eviction should exhibit a comparable phase gradient.
It does not: random eviction fails seven of eight paired permutation tests across both models (7/8 FAIL); the single exception (Qwen $s{=}0.30$, $p{=}0.012$) exhibits negligible effect size ($d_z{=}{-}0.04$), producing no practically meaningful phase-modulated severity. % exp_id: bf16_ds_rand_s015..s030, bf16_qw_rand_s015..s030; verdict: 7/8 FAIL, 1 PASS (qw_rand_s030 p=0.012 d=-0.035 negligible)
The absence of a phase gradient under random masking isolates the amplification as strategy-specific: it arises from the interaction between importance-based eviction and phase structure, not from compound sparsity per se.

\paragraph{Cross-model replication and magnitude asymmetry.}
The phase-strategy interaction replicates across both models with perfect ordinal agreement: the Spearman rank correlation of paired $d_z$ effect sizes across sparsity levels is $\rho{=}1.0$, and a gradient permutation test confirms this monotonic co-escalation ($p{=}0.043$). % exp_id: cross_model_correlation; Spearman rho=1.0, gradient_perm p=0.043
All eight paired Wilcoxon tests (4 sparsity levels $\times$ 2 models) reject $H_0$, confirming the pattern is not an artifact of a single model's weight structure.

The \emph{magnitude} of the effect, however, differs substantially.
Qwen's median severity differences ($0.039 \to 0.235 \to 1.268 \to 2.943$) are approximately one-fifth of DeepSeek's ($0.39 \to 1.48 \to 7.16 \to 14.59$), and the onset threshold differs: DeepSeek's gradient is significant from $s{=}0.15$ (paired $d_z{=}0.44$), while Qwen's becomes clearly significant only at $s \geq 0.20$ ($d_z{=}0.55$; $s{=}0.15$ is borderline at $d_z{=}0.28$ with CI crossing zero). % exp_id: cohens_d_bf16.json (ds d_z: 0.4416,0.5195,0.6831,0.8031), cohens_d_bf16_qwen.json (qw d_z: 0.2811,0.5494,0.8894,1.0220).
The two models share the Qwen2ForCausalLM architecture but differ in training: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B is distilled from a larger reasoning model, while Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct undergoes standard instruction tuning.
We conjecture that distillation amplifies the phase-strategy interaction by producing sharper internal phase transitions---a hypothesis testable by comparing distilled and non-distilled variants at matched scale.

\paragraph{Mechanistic evidence: discrimination collapse as the robust signal.}
The entropy-discrimination collapse hypothesis (\S\ref{sec:analysis}) receives partial cross-model support.
The discrimination components---Gini coefficient reduction and coefficient-of-variation compression under compound sparsity---are directionally consistent across both models, confirming that importance-based eviction loses discriminative power in low-sparsity phases regardless of training procedure.
However, the entropy component is model-dependent: DeepSeek exhibits consistent negative entropy shifts (attention concentrates further under head pruning), while Qwen shows a sign reversal at $s{=}0.25$ ($\Delta H {=} {+}0.045$) and near-zero shift at $s{=}0.30$ ($\Delta H {=} {-}0.007$). % exp_id: mechanism_entropy_qwen; s025: +0.045, s030: -0.007
This divergence suggests that discrimination collapse---not entropy redistribution---is the primary driver of the phase-strategy interaction, with entropy behavior being a model-dependent secondary effect.
We therefore characterize the mechanistic evidence as \emph{preliminary}: the discrimination pathway is robust across models, but the complete entropy-discrimination collapse narrative requires the qualification that its entropy component does not generalize.

\paragraph{Implications for compound sparsity deployment.}
Our findings suggest that the standard practice of applying a uniform compression budget across all inference steps is suboptimal for reasoning models.
Compound severity is not distributed evenly: it concentrates in low-sparsity phases, where the entropy-discrimination collapse mechanism (\S\ref{sec:analysis}) renders importance-based eviction unreliable.
A deployment pipeline that allocates the same sparsity level $s$ to every token position implicitly accepts order-of-magnitude severity penalties during the exploratory reasoning stages that happen to fall in the low-sparsity regime.

This observation motivates \emph{phase-aware compression budgets}: rather than a single global sparsity target, the system would allocate higher capacity (lower sparsity) to low-sparsity phases---where compound interaction is most severe---and reclaim that budget in high-sparsity phases, where compound behavior is near-additive and importance-based eviction remains effective.
The severity gradient $G$ reported in \S\ref{sec:phase-amplification} provides a natural signal for such allocation: phases with $G \gg 1$ receive a reduced sparsity budget, while phases with $G \leq 1$ tolerate aggressive compression with minimal quality loss.

\paragraph{Future directions.}
The phase-aware allocation principle above points toward a concrete system design: a \emph{phase-gated controller} that monitors attention sparsity statistics in real time and dynamically adjusts the compound sparsity budget per reasoning phase.
The controller would route each generation step through a low-overhead phase classifier (\S\ref{sec:phase-seg}), then apply a phase-specific sparsity configuration derived from the severity gradient.
Whether such a controller can recover most of the compression benefit while avoiding the severity amplification in low-sparsity phases is an open empirical question.

A second direction concerns completing the mechanistic picture.
The discrimination collapse component of our hypothesis is robust across models, but the entropy redistribution component is model-dependent (\S\ref{sec:analysis}).
Directly measuring per-head entropy shifts across architecturally distinct models---and identifying what training-time properties (e.g., distillation depth, RLHF intensity) determine whether entropy concentrates or disperses under head pruning---would clarify the boundary conditions of the full entropy-discrimination collapse mechanism.

Finally, scaling the empirical methodology to larger models and diverse reasoning tasks would establish the generality of the phase-strategy interaction documented in this work.

\subsection{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

\paragraph{Model scale.}
All experiments are conducted at the 7B parameter scale.
Whether the phase-modulated severity patterns persist, amplify, or attenuate at larger scales (e.g., 70B) remains untested.
Larger models may exhibit different attention redundancy structures that alter the discrimination collapse dynamics (and the model-dependent entropy component may behave differently at scale).
% REVIEWER-ATTACK: "7B is too small to be relevant for production."
% REBUTTAL: 7B is the most-deployed scale for on-device and cost-constrained serving—exactly where compound sparsity is needed. The mechanism (entropy-discrimination collapse) is scale-agnostic in principle. Scaling experiments are future work.

\paragraph{Architectural scope.}
Our two models---DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct---share the Qwen2ForCausalLM architecture.
The cross-model replication (\S\ref{sec:cross-model}) confirms that the findings are not artifacts of a single model's weights, but both models share the same attention mechanism design.
The entropy-discrimination collapse mechanism is in principle agnostic across attention architectures (it depends on attention redistribution, not architecture-specific components), but empirical validation on architecturally distinct attention designs (e.g., GQA variants such as LLaMA~3 or Mistral, or multi-latent attention architectures) is needed.
% REVIEWER-ATTACK: "Cross-model ≠ cross-architecture. Both are Qwen2ForCausalLM."
% REBUTTAL: Correct—we explicitly state this is cross-model (different training: distillation vs instruction tuning), not cross-architecture. The two models isolate the training variable while controlling architecture. Cross-architecture validation (LLaMA, Mistral) is acknowledged as future work.

\paragraph{Task coverage.}
We evaluate exclusively on MATH-500, a mathematical reasoning benchmark.
Different reasoning tasks---code generation, commonsense reasoning, multi-hop question answering---may induce different phase structures with different sparsity distributions, potentially altering the severity gradient profile.
Generalizing the phase-strategy interaction to broader reasoning domains is an important next step.
% REVIEWER-ATTACK: "Only MATH-500. How do we know this isn't a math-specific artifact?"
% REBUTTAL: The mechanism (entropy-discrimination collapse under head pruning) depends on attention distribution properties, not math-specific features. MATH-500 is a standard benchmark with diverse difficulty. However, different reasoning tasks may induce different phase structures—we state this limitation explicitly rather than overclaiming.

\paragraph{Statistical scope.}
Bootstrap confidence intervals use $B{=}10{,}000$ resamples. The paired permutation test yields $n{=}49$ paired problems for DeepSeek (1 excluded) and $n{=}46$ for Qwen (4 excluded). % exp_id: cohens_d_bf16.json, cohens_d_bf16_qwen.json
The severity difference distribution is right-skewed (mean/median ratio ${\sim}1.6{:}1$ at $s{=}0.30$), motivating our use of medians and nonparametric tests rather than parametric alternatives. % exp_id: bf16_importance_s030; mean_diff=22.94, median_diff=14.59 (segment-level). Per-problem paired: median_diff=9.9436 at s030
All four permutation tests reject $H_0$ after Bonferroni correction ($p_{\text{Bonf}} < 0.005$; Table~\ref{tab:permutation}), with CI lower bounds increasing from $0.19$ to $6.70$---confirming the effect direction at every sparsity level. The permutation CIs at higher sparsity are wider (e.g., $[6.70,\; 16.29]$ at $s{=}0.30$), reflecting genuine variance in per-problem severity amplification. % exp_id: permutation_test_results.json; permutation CIs: s015=[0.19,0.62], s020=[0.69,1.49], s025=[1.66,6.64], s030=[6.70,16.29]

A notable exception among the random baselines is the Qwen random condition at $s{=}0.30$, which yields a statistically significant result ($p{=}0.012$) despite negligible effect size ($d_z{=}{-}0.04$, bootstrap CI excluding zero). % exp_id: qw_rand_s030; B=10000, p=0.012, d=-0.035, negligible
This case illustrates that dichotomous significance testing can flag effects of no practical magnitude---reinforcing the importance of reporting effect sizes and confidence intervals alongside $p$-values.

\paragraph{Sparsity range.}
Our experiments span $s \in \{0.15, 0.20, 0.25, 0.30\}$, a moderate range representative of practical deployment targets.
More extreme sparsity ($s > 0.50$) may exhibit qualitatively different interaction dynamics---the sub-exponential growth pattern suggests the severity gradient may plateau, but this remains unverified.
Conversely, the lower boundary at which phase-modulated amplification first emerges is not yet characterized.
% REVIEWER-ATTACK: "Why not test higher sparsity? 0.30 is conservative."
% REBUTTAL: Our focus is on the practically relevant regime where models retain usable quality. At s>0.30 both strategies degrade severely, making II measurement less informative. The sub-exponential growth (C6, $\Delta$ growth rate $3.8{\times} \to 4.8{\times} \to 2.0{\times}$) suggests saturation at higher sparsity, but confirming this is future work.

\paragraph{No throughput evaluation.}
This work focuses on characterizing the \emph{structural} properties of compound sparsity severity---its phase dependence, strategy dependence, and interaction magnitude.
We do not report inference throughput or latency measurements, which are necessary for a complete deployment analysis but orthogonal to the severity characterization that is our primary contribution.
% REVIEWER-ATTACK: "No system evaluation. How do we know the severity amplification matters for real deployment?"
% REBUTTAL: This is an empirical finding paper, not a method/system paper. The contribution is characterizing *what happens* (phase-modulated severity) and *why* (entropy-discrimination collapse), not building a system to fix it. Phase-gated controllers are explicitly scoped as future work. The finding is actionable regardless: any compound sparsity deployment should be aware of phase-dependent severity.
TEXEOF

\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}

We presented an empirical investigation of how compound sparsity severity---the super-additive interaction between attention head pruning and KV cache eviction---varies across reasoning phases and eviction strategies in 7B-parameter language models. Our central finding is that compound severity is not a fixed property of the sparsity level but an emergent phase-strategy interaction whose magnitude spans over an order of magnitude within a single generation.

Our contributions, mapped to confirmed claims, are:
\begin{enumerate}[nosep,leftmargin=*]
    \item \textbf{Strategy dependence (C1).} Compound severity depends qualitatively on the eviction strategy: importance-based eviction produces phase-modulated interaction (median phase difference $0.39$--$14.59$), while random eviction shows no significant phase modulation in 7/8 conditions (the sole exception---Qwen $s{=}0.30$, $p{=}0.012$, $d_z{=}{-}0.04$---has negligible effect size).

    \item \textbf{Phase modulation (C2).} Under importance-based eviction, the median Interaction Index difference between low- and high-sparsity phases increases monotonically with sparsity (Bonferroni-corrected $p < 0.005$ at all four levels), with paired effect sizes growing from $d_z{=}0.44$ (small) to $d_z{=}0.80$ (large).

    \item \textbf{Phase-strategy crossover (C3).} At $s{=}0.25$, importance-based eviction simultaneously outperforms random in high-sparsity phases ($\widetilde{\mathrm{II}} = 0.032$ vs.\ $0.818$) and underperforms in low-sparsity phases ($\widetilde{\mathrm{II}} = 7.196$ vs.\ $1.363$)---a qualitative reversal in strategy ranking.

    \item \textbf{Sub-exponential growth (C6).} The severity gradient grows with sparsity but at a decelerating rate, suggesting a natural ceiling on phase-dependent amplification.

    \item \textbf{Cross-model replication (C5).} The monotonic gradient replicates on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct at $s \geq 0.20$ ($d_z \geq 0.55$; Spearman $\rho = 1.0$ across sparsity levels; gradient permutation $p = 0.043$), with attenuated absolute magnitude (${\sim}1/5$ of DeepSeek).

    \item \textbf{Mechanistic explanation (C4).} Discrimination collapse---whereby head pruning degrades the discriminative power of importance scores---is robustly confirmed across both models (Gini and CV decrease in all 16 conditions). A secondary entropy redistribution pattern is consistent for DeepSeek but partially replicates on Qwen (2/4 conditions), indicating model-dependent modulation.
\end{enumerate}

\paragraph{Limitations.}
Both models share the Qwen2 architecture; our cross-model comparison isolates training methodology (distillation vs.\ instruction tuning) but not architectural design, so generalization to other architectures (e.g., LLaMA, Mistral, multi-latent attention) remains open.
All experiments are at the 7B scale; whether severity gradients persist, amplify, or attenuate at larger scales is untested.
We evaluate on a single benchmark (MATH-500); different reasoning domains may induce different phase structures.
The discrimination collapse mechanism is supported by correlational evidence but lacks direct causal validation through controlled entropy manipulation.
While discrimination collapse (Gini and CV reduction) is consistent across all conditions for both models, the entropy redistribution component replicates on only 2 of 4 sparsity levels for Qwen, suggesting model-specific factors modulate its manifestation.

\paragraph{Future work.}
A \emph{phase-gated sparsity controller} that dynamically adjusts compound sparsity budgets per reasoning phase could mitigate the severity amplification we document while preserving compression gains where compound behavior is near-additive.
Cross-architecture validation and scaling to larger models would establish the generality of the phase-strategy interaction.
Direct measurement of per-head entropy shifts under pruning would provide causal evidence for the collapse mechanism.
